criterion_notes.c1: Examines the production cost structure and economies of scale of municipal potable water utilities (Large Water Suppliers) in Japan, rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Coverage ratio enters only as a right-hand-side hedonic output quality adjustment in the cost function (alongside descriptive national trends in Table 2).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — examines municipal and public water utility consolidation following the 1999 amendment to Japan's Municipal Merger Law (the Great Heisei Era Consolidation), which is a legal, administrative and institutional reform. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — consolidation is analyzed strictly as an industrial-organization scale restructuring affecting utility production costs and bulk-water purchasing costs, rather than as a rule-type mechanism or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing household service access, eligibility, connection, or consumer tariffs. Note that even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is still excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4 (wrong outcome).
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical panel study estimating hedonic translog cost functions and input cost share equations via seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) across 12,952 utility-year observations (6,648 consolidated and 6,304 non-consolidated water utility observations) from FY1999 to FY2006.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports utility-level total production costs, input cost shares (labour, capital, other), long-run economies of scale, and Allen-Uzawa partial elasticities of substitution. Does not report outcomes measuring household or community access, connection, continuity, reliability, consumer affordability/tariffs, or exclusion; the authors explicitly note that potential merger effects on services to groups such as the poor were not examined.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (public Large Water Suppliers in Japan, FY1999-FY2006, n=12,952 utility-year observations), exposure (utility consolidation following local government mergers, captured by consolidation dummies), outcome (total production cost, input shares, and scale economies), and study design (panel econometric translog hedonic cost-function analysis) are clearly specified.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper looks at the economic effects of consolidation of Japanese water utilities in the period 1999–2006 using translog cost functions with a hedonic output specification. The results clarify what factors have been most affected in terms of the cost structure of the water utilities after consolidation.

In 1999, the Municipal Merger Law was amended so that local governments could be consolidated into large authorities (known as the Great Heisei Era Consolidation). Subsequently, many neighbouring WSSs have merged or been taken over; for example, the number of LWSs fell from 1958 in 2000 to 1602 in 2005 (Table 2).
The number of observations for each year (FY1999–FY2006) is summarised in Table 3. In summary, the number of observations was 6648 for CWUs and 6304 for NWUs.
Total cost (C) is sum of labour cost, capital cost and other input costs. Therefore, the cost shares of each input (Sl, Sk, So) are obtained by dividing each input cost by total cost.

It is possible that other benefits of mergers may not be reflected in the results, such as improved billing and metering and improved services to particular groups in society, such as the poor. Further research could usefully investigate any such effects.

raw_response.exposure: Consolidation of municipally owned Large Water Suppliers following the 1999 amendment of Japan's Municipal Merger Law (Great Heisei Era Consolidation), measured via post-consolidation and consolidated-utility dummy variables.
raw_response.outcome: Utility-level total production cost, input cost shares (labour, capital, and other inputs), economies of scale, and Allen-Uzawa partial elasticities of substitution.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Publicly owned Large Water Suppliers (potable water utilities serving over 5,001 people) in Japan from FY1999 to FY2006: 12,952 utility-year observations (6,648 consolidated water utility observations and 6,304 non-consolidated water utility observations; 859 observations excluded for missing data).
raw_response.rationale: This econometric panel study evaluates how municipal water utility mergers in Japan (1999–2006) affected utility-level production costs, input cost shares, and economies of scale using a hedonic translog cost function. Coverage ratio and per-capita daily water supplied appear only as right-hand-side hedonic output adjustments in the cost model rather than as access outcomes, and the authors explicitly note that consumer service impacts (such as improved services to the poor) were outside the study's scope. Accordingly, the paper is excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome), and also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2 because consolidation is studied as an industrial-scale cost restructuring rather than a rule or regulatory structure directly governing household service access.
raw_response.study_design: Quantitative panel econometric study estimating hedonic translog cost functions and input share equations via seemingly unrelated regression (SUR).
